questions.statement: What position does the author take?
questions.context: Text: 'Some people say the country should build more roads. Roads cost money, take up land and encourage longer car journeys; without them, most journeys would be shorter and cheaper.'

options.text: Against building more roads
options.feedback: Every point listed counts against new roads, which reveals an opposing position.

options.text: In favour of building more roads
options.feedback: An author arguing for roads would list benefits rather than costs.

options.text: Neutral, because the author never takes a side
options.feedback: The consistent direction of the arguments shows a position, even though the word 'oppose' is absent.

options.text: In favour of replacing roads with railways
options.feedback: Railways are never mentioned, so the author is not proposing an alternative transport mode.

questions.explanation:
A position can be detected from the direction of the evidence even when no explicit verdict appears. Listing only disadvantages of a proposal is itself a stance.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What criticism is the text making?
questions.context: Text: 'Every year the city spends a great deal on traffic signs. Almost nobody has ever asked whether the signs are in the right places.'

options.text: The city spends money without checking whether the spending is useful
options.feedback: Spending is presented as routine while the question of its value is raised but ignored, which is the criticism.

options.text: The city spends too little on traffic signs
options.feedback: The text criticises unchecked spending, not the amount spent.

options.text: The city has too many traffic accidents
options.feedback: No accident figures appear anywhere in the text.

options.text: The city should remove all traffic signs
options.feedback: Removing signs is a conclusion the text does not draw; it questions placement rather than existence.

questions.explanation:
Critical texts often express criticism through the gap between what is done and what is examined. Naming that gap is more accurate than supplying a conclusion the writer never reached.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should a critical reader notice about this evidence?
questions.context: Text: 'The proposal would certainly help farmers, and everyone in the room smiled when it was announced.'

options.text: It reports reactions rather than results, and reactions prove nothing about effectiveness
options.feedback: A smile measures approval in the moment, which is a different question from whether a policy improves incomes.

options.text: It proves the proposal works, because the room responded well
options.feedback: A favourable reaction does not establish an outcome that the text never reports.

options.text: It shows that the proposal was rejected later
options.feedback: The text records approval rather than rejection.

options.text: It shows that farmers were present in the room
options.feedback: The room is not identified as containing farmers, so that cannot be concluded.

questions.explanation:
Critical analysis asks what kind of evidence a text offers. Reactions are evidence about perceptions, not about effects, and confusing the two is a common reading error.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why is the absence of a cost figure significant?
questions.context: Text: 'The programme ran for two years and reached four hundred people. Its total cost is not stated anywhere in the report.'

options.text: Without a cost, the value of the programme cannot be assessed
options.feedback: A programme's value depends on what it achieved against what it required, so a missing cost blocks any assessment of efficiency.

options.text: The cost is unimportant for judging a social programme
options.feedback: Cost is precisely what makes efficiency measurable, so dismissing it removes the only comparison available.

options.text: The cost was zero
options.feedback: Nothing in the text states that no money was spent.

options.text: The cost was considered too sensitive to publish
options.feedback: The reason for the omission is not given, and inventing one would go beyond the text.

questions.explanation:
Critiquing a text does not require accusing it of deception. Noting which necessary information is absent is a precise and defensible observation about its limitations.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What kind of text does this passage represent?
questions.context: Text: 'Some people believe that the new stadium will attract tourists. Others argue that it will simply cost the city money it needs for schools.'

options.text: A text presenting two opposed positions without choosing one
options.feedback: Two statements joined by opposing framing present a debate and settle nothing.

options.text: A text arguing strongly for the stadium
options.feedback: Neither view is endorsed, so the passage is not an argument for the stadium.

options.text: A text reporting the outcome of the stadium project
options.feedback: The stadium is still a proposal here, so no outcome is reported.

options.text: A text explaining how stadiums are financed
options.feedback: No financing mechanism appears in the text.

questions.explanation:
Recognising whether a text argues, reports or merely presents alternatives changes how a reader should evaluate it. A balanced text cannot be criticised for a conclusion it deliberately avoids.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What kind of evidence supports the claim about the scheme?
questions.context: Text: 'The scheme reduced illness in the villages where it was introduced. Villages not covered by the scheme experienced no such reduction during the same period.'

options.text: A comparison between treated and untreated places over the same period
options.feedback: Comparing two groups that differed in exposure but not in time is the structure of an experimental comparison.

options.text: A list of official opinions supporting the scheme
options.feedback: No opinions are quoted anywhere in the text.

options.text: A calculation of how much the scheme cost
options.feedback: Cost is not mentioned and would not be evidence of effectiveness.

options.text: A description of how the scheme was designed
options.feedback: Design describes how the scheme works rather than showing that it worked.

questions.explanation:
Evidence type matters more than evidence volume. A controlled comparison supports a causal claim in a way that an opinion or a cost figure never can.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What weakness does this text reveal in its own evidence?
questions.context: Text: 'Experts agree that the new building is impressive. When asked to justify the claim, most of them mentioned the design alone.'

options.text: The experts rely on one aspect, so the general agreement covers only that aspect
options.feedback: If every justification rests on the design, the claim of expert agreement is agreement about one narrow point presented as a general verdict.

options.text: The experts disagree among themselves about the design
options.feedback: The text reports agreement rather than disagreement.

options.text: The design is not impressive in fact
options.feedback: The text presents the design as the basis of the praise, so this reverses its content.

options.text: No experts were consulted at all
options.feedback: Experts are quoted throughout, so the last reading contradicts the passage.

questions.explanation:
A claim wider than the evidence supporting it is a common defect in persuasive writing. This item asks the student to compare the scope of a conclusion with the scope of the reasons given.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the contrast between the first two sentences produce?
questions.context: Text: 'Nobody wants another shopping centre. Yet three more opened in the region last year, and rents in every nearby village have risen.'

options.text: It sets a stated preference against an opposite trend in practice
options.feedback: The opening states a lack of demand while the second reports three openings and rising rents, producing an unresolved contradiction.

options.text: It shows that village rents caused the shopping centres to open
options.feedback: The second sentence reports an outcome of the openings rather than their cause.

options.text: It confirms that the first sentence is factually wrong
options.feedback: The text leaves the contradiction open rather than resolving it against the first sentence.

options.text: It argues that nobody should rent in the region
options.feedback: Nothing in the text suggests that anyone should avoid renting.

questions.explanation:
A text can contain a tension without resolving it, and noticing that tension is more useful than forcing a conclusion. The contradiction here may be the author's point or simply the puzzle of the passage.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the repeated figurative expression accomplish?
questions.context: Text: 'The writer describes the old market as a living record of how the town ate, traded and argued. She uses the word twice more in the paragraph, each time in the same sense.'

options.text: It builds a consistent picture of the market as something alive and communal
options.feedback: A phrase about eating, trading and arguing makes the market a living presence, and repetition reinforces that image.

options.text: It gives the market a literal documentary purpose
options.feedback: The expression is figurative and does not describe a documentary function.

options.text: It criticises the market as chaotic
options.feedback: The word 'record' is neutral and the description is affectionate rather than critical.

options.text: It compares the market with a written archive only
options.feedback: The image is an extended metaphor about a whole way of life, not a simple comparison with a written archive.

questions.explanation:
Repetition of a figurative phrase is a rhetorical choice that builds meaning cumulatively. Tracking where a metaphor appears and how it develops is part of analysing a text critically.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the most substantial criticism available?
questions.context: Text: 'The article claims that a change in the diet of the population explains the rise in a disease. It gives no information about what that diet was before the change or about other possible causes.'

options.text: The explanation is offered without the baseline or the alternatives it would need
options.feedback: Without a before-and-after comparison and a consideration of other causes, the explanation cannot be evaluated.

options.text: The article is written in an unsuitable register
options.feedback: Register is not the issue described in the text.

options.text: The article is too short to be published
options.feedback: Length does not determine whether an argument is adequately supported.

options.text: The disease is not mentioned often enough
options.feedback: Frequency of mention is not a measure of argumentative adequacy.

questions.explanation:
Substantive criticism concerns the relationship between a claim and its evidence. This item separates that kind of critique from the cosmetic observations that often pass for analysis.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the significance of the two words?
questions.context: Text: 'The author writes that the plan was 'unambitious'. Later in the same article, the same plan is described as 'realistic' given the resources available.

options.text: They are evaluative and carry opposite judgements depending on the standard applied
options.feedback: 'Unambitious' judges the plan against a maximal standard and 'realistic' judges it against what was achievable, so the difference lies in the criterion.

options.text: They are synonyms and reinforce the same judgement
options.feedback: The two words convey opposite evaluations rather than the same one.

options.text: They are factual descriptions with no evaluative content
options.feedback: Both are judgements rather than measurements, so they are not merely factual.

options.text: They show that the author changed his mind about the plan
options.feedback: Applying two standards to one plan is not the same as changing an opinion about it.

questions.explanation:
Evaluative words in criticism carry a standard with them. Reading them critically means asking what standard makes a judgement fair, which is what the item sets the student to do.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should a critical reader take from this pairing of photograph and caption?
questions.context: Text: 'A photograph shows a line of people waiting outside a clinic. The caption reads: 'Residents queue for medical care in the capital.' The date on the image is ten years old.

options.text: The caption describes the scene accurately but the image may not represent conditions now
options.feedback: A precise caption paired with an old photograph can mislead a reader about the present, because the description sounds current.

options.text: The caption was written ten years ago and is therefore worthless
options.feedback: An old caption remains informative about its own time, so it is not worthless.

options.text: The photograph proves that conditions have not changed
options.feedback: The date cannot prove that conditions are unchanged; the opposite reading is equally available.

options.text: The date was added later to make the image look recent
options.feedback: The text gives no basis for accusing anyone of manipulating the date.

questions.explanation:
Images and captions are separate claims that must be evaluated separately. Noticing that a description may be accurate yet outdated is a habit of careful reading that applies well beyond photographs.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the omission of the reply suggest about the newspaper's treatment of the claim?
questions.context: Text: 'The newspaper printed a letter claiming that a factory discharges waste into the river. The factory replied the next day, and the newspaper did not report the reply.

options.text: The newspaper published an allegation without giving the other party a chance as it presents the story
options.feedback: Publishing a damaging allegation and leaving a published reply unreported shows a one-sided presentation.

options.text: The newspaper was not interested in the story at all
options.feedback: Reporting a claim indicates interest in the story rather than the absence of it.

options.text: The reply must have supported the factory completely
options.feedback: The content of the reply is unknown, so its supposed support cannot be inferred.

options.text: The newspaper believed the reply was unimportant
options.feedback: The text describes an omission, not a judgement that the reply was unimportant.

questions.explanation:
Balance is a testable property of reporting. What a source omits, and in what order, is often more revealing about its stance than what it states.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What conflict of interest does this reveal?
questions.context: Text: 'The report was written by a committee whose members all work in the same industry. It recommends measures that would affect their own companies'

options.text: Those who would be affected by the recommendations helped write them
options.feedback: When the people deciding what to recommend are among the people who gain or lose from it, the assessment of benefit is not independent.

options.text: The committee was too small to be representative
options.feedback: Size is a separate question from independence, and the text does not raise it.

options.text: The recommendations were written in an informal register
options.feedback: Nothing in the text concerns the register of the recommendations.

options.text: The industry has no legal obligation to follow them
options.feedback: No legal obligation is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

questions.explanation:
Evaluating a source includes asking who produced it and what their interests are. This is the standard first question in media and research literacy, and it applies to any text that recommends something.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What two questions would a critical reader ask about this claim?
questions.context: Text: 'The article claims the new system 'works better in every way' and offers no comparison with the old one and no definition of 'better'.

options.text: Better than what, and measured how?
options.feedback: A sweeping comparative claim requires a comparison and a criterion, and the text supplies neither.

options.text: Who wrote it, and how long is it?
options.feedback: Authorship and length bear on credibility and presentation, not on whether the comparison holds.

options.text: Where was it published, and by whom?
options.feedback: Publication details identify the source rather than test the substance of the claim.

options.text: Is it long, and is it expensive?
options.feedback: Length and cost are irrelevant to the meaning of a comparative claim about performance.

questions.explanation:
Two questions cover most sweeping claims: what is it being compared with, and by what measure. This item asks the student to produce them rather than judge the outcome, which is the reusable skill.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the most serious problem with this evidence?
questions.context: Text: A blog post argues that remote work must be permanent, citing a single survey of volunteers who had already chosen to work that way.

options.text: The people surveyed had already selected the arrangement being praised
options.feedback: People who chose a mode of work are not a neutral sample for judging whether everyone should adopt it, so the group is biased from the start.

options.text: The survey was conducted too recently
options.feedback: Recency is not the weakness; the problem lies in how the sample was formed.

options.text: The blog post is too short
options.feedback: Length does not determine the validity of evidence.

options.text: Remote work is not mentioned often enough
options.feedback: Frequency of a term is not a measure of argumentative strength.

questions.explanation:
A biased sample cannot be corrected by a larger number of responses. This item asks the student to name the defect in how the evidence was gathered rather than in how it was reported.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What kind of language appears in the discrepancy?
questions.context: Text: 'The brochure promises that the tour visits three communities. In practice, guests pass through two of them without stopping and only dine in the third.'

options.text: Promotional language that overstates what the experience delivers
options.feedback: A brochure is an advertisement, and 'visits' implies a contact that the actual itinerary does not deliver.

options.text: Legal language designed to bind the company
options.feedback: Legal obligation would require reference to terms or conditions, and none appears.

options.text: Technical language describing a research method
options.feedback: No method is being described in a brochure.

options.text: Satirical language mocking the tourists
options.feedback: There is no mocking tone in either the text or the description.

questions.explanation:
Comparing a claim with the practice it describes is one of the sharpest forms of critical reading. This item asks the student to name the register of the overstated text as well as the defect.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the disagreement suggest about the ruling?
questions.context: Text: 'Two commentaries on the same ruling disagree. One says the court expanded access to the remedy. The other says the court left the law exactly as it was.'

options.text: Its meaning depends on which parts of it each reader emphasises
options.feedback: Two readings of the same document producing opposite descriptions shows that its operative language leaves room for interpretation.

options.text: One of the two commentators must be lying
options.feedback: Disagreement between commentators is common on contested rulings and does not establish deception.

options.text: The ruling was issued by two different courts
options.feedback: The passage describes one ruling discussed by two people, not two courts.

options.text: The ruling has no text that can be read
options.feedback: A written ruling exists and is precisely what both commentators read.

questions.explanation:
Disagreement about a document is evidence about the document's ambiguity rather than about the honesty of its readers. This distinction is central to critical analysis of any institutional text.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How should these two adjectives be treated?
questions.context: Text: 'The article describes the neighbourhood as 'quiet and authentic'. No data support the word quiet, and no evidence is offered for authentic.'

options.text: As unsupported evaluations rather than as descriptions that can be verified
options.feedback: 'Quiet' and 'authentic' are value judgements presented as descriptions, and neither is measurable as stated.

options.text: As precise technical terms with agreed definitions
options.feedback: Neither word is a technical term with an agreed definition in this context.

options.text: As quotations from residents that require no support
options.feedback: No one is quoted, so the adjectives are not attributable to a speaker.

options.text: As evidence that the article favours the neighbourhood
options.feedback: The presence of favourable words does show a preference, but the item asks how to treat them as evidence.

questions.explanation:
Evaluating language means separating descriptive claims that can be checked from judgements that cannot. Naming the two kinds precisely is more useful than merely calling the text biased.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the strongest conclusion a careful reader can draw?
questions.context: Text: A reviewer says a book is 'the first account of the period in Spanish'. The publisher's page says a book with a similar title appeared three years earlier in Spanish.

options.text: The reviewer's claim of priority is contradicted by an existing earlier book
options.feedback: A claim of being the first is checkable, and a documented earlier book of the same kind defeats it.

options.text: The reviewer must have misread the earlier book
options.feedback: The reviewer's claim is unsupported, but no reason exists to assume a misreading rather than an error of information.

options.text: The publisher's page must be wrong
options.feedback: Nothing in the description favours the publisher's page over the reviewer's statement.

options.text: Both books may be useful despite the disagreement
options.feedback: The usefulness of the books is beside the point, because the issue is a verifiable claim about priority.

questions.explanation: Critical analysis distinguishes claims that can be checked from opinions that cannot. This item asks the student to identify which kind of claim a priority statement is, and what follows when the check fails.
questions.subject: ingles
